title: Time is a stream
hookLine: time is but the stream I go a-fishing in (Walden 2)

cards: Calendars, deadlines, a phone that buzzes on the hour, an app that tells you how long you looked at your phone. On a busy day, time is a thing to manage: spent, saved, wasted, killed.
Yesterday Thoreau was keeping careful records of the seasons. Today, in the same book, he picks time up and turns it into something completely different. Not a budget.
A stream. And he goes fishing in it.

teach.b: From Walden's second chapter: "Time is but the stream I go a-fishing in. I drink at it; but while I drink I see the sandy bottom and detect how shallow it is. Its thin current slides away, but eternity remains. I would drink deeper; fish in the sky, whose bottom is pebbly with stars."
First, a stream, not a clock. You don't own or spend a stream. You go to it, sit beside it, fish in it, which mostly means waiting.
Second, the shallow bottom. Looked at closely, time is thin. The minutes really do slide away, and he doesn't pretend otherwise.
Third, but eternity remains. Under the thin current, something doesn't slide. He doesn't define it; he just says it remains.
Readers hear different things in that word: God, nature, the timeless, the present moment itself. The sentence leaves room for each of them. Fourth, the sky full of stars.
Then he flips the picture: he'd drink deeper, and fish in the sky. The stream becomes the night sky; the shallow bed, a floor of stars.
It's a strange image, and it works by feel more than logic: the thin water of hours, opening onto something vast.
And it suggests another way to be with time: not always counting it, sometimes sitting beside it, line in the water, letting it run.

how: Some readers take Thoreau's stream as an invitation to spend some time uncounted, sitting beside the hours rather than managing them.

games.q: what does “time is a stream” mean?
o: a fishing trip Thoreau took on the Concord River
time as a shallow stream with eternity beneath it
a warning that time flies and can't be wasted

games.q: inside the stream: tap the pairs.
p: the stream I go a-fishing in

s: Thoreau calls time a stream he goes fishing in
"Time is but the stream I go a-fishing in."
he says the stream of time is endlessly deep
he sees the sandy bottom and detects how shallow it is.
the passage ends at the bottom of the stream

games.q: you're Thoreau, drinking from the stream of time, and you see how shallow it is. what do you want next?
o: to get out of the stream.
to drink deeper and fish in the sky.
games.why: "I would drink deeper; fish in the sky, whose bottom is pebbly with stars."

practice: For now, don't count anything, not breaths, not seconds, not how long is left; if your phone is near, turn it face down.
Let time go by like water past a bank, noticing the sounds and small shifts in your body without catching any of them. If you find yourself counting, smile and let the count float off downstream.

wordCard.voice: Time is a stream. Thoreau's picture of time as water he fishes in: shallow, sliding away, and yet with eternity under it. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: the stream. You're not spending these minutes; you're sitting beside them. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Walden, ch. 2, Where I Lived, and What I Lived For
